D-SMART: Enhancing LLM Dialogue Consistency via
Dynamic Structured Memory And Reasoning Tree

Xiang Lei    Qin Li ††thanks: Correspondence to: Qin Li $¡$qli@sei.ecnu.edu.cn$¿$.    Min Zhang    Min Zhang
Abstract

Large Language Models (LLMs) often exhibit factual inconsistencies and logical decay in extended, multi-turn dialogues, a challenge stemming from their reliance on static, pre-trained knowledge and an inability to reason adaptively over the dialogue history. Prevailing mitigation strategies, such as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and agentic working memories, improve information recall but still engage with fundamentally static knowledge sources and follow pre-defined single reasoning path. This hinders their ability to preserve factual and logical consistency of their responses in multi-turn dialogues while the context evolves over time. To address this issue, we propose D-SMART, a model-agnostic framework designed to maintain multi-turn dialogue consistency by enabling LLMs to build and reason over a dynamic, structured representation of the conversational context. This is achieved via two synergistic components: (1) a Dynamic Structured Memory (DSM), which incrementally constructs and maintains an authoritative, OWL-compliant knowledge graph of the conversation; and (2) a Reasoning Tree (RT), which executes inferences as an explicit and traceable multi-step search over the graph. As the popular-used quality score (judged by GPT-4) can overlook logical flaws, we introduce new NLI-based metrics to better measure multi-turn dialogue consistency. Comprehensive experiments on the MT-Bench-101 benchmark show that D-SMART significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, elevating the dialogue consistency score by over 48% for both proprietary and open-source models, and notably improves the quality score of the latter by up to 10.1%.

1 Shanghai Key Laboratory of Trustworthy Computing,

East China Normal University,

Shanghai, China

Introduction

While Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across various tasks (Li et al. 2024), maintaining logical and factual consistency in extended, multi-turn dialogues remains a significant challenge (Yi et al. 2024). Lapses in this consistency can severely undermine effective information conveyance, intention clarification, and consensus building (She et al. 2024). However, the architectural foundations of contemporary LLMs often struggle to meet this critical requirement, especially as dialogues become longer and more complex (Liu et al. 2023; Huang et al. 2025).

This challenge stems from a fundamental reliance on static, pre-trained knowledge and the processing of an unstructured dialogue history, where attention to prior turns can decay (Hu et al. 2024; Zhao et al. 2024). This can lead to difficulties in resolving context ambiguity, managing conflicts between the model’s internal knowledge and newly introduced dialogue-specific facts (Xu et al. 2024a), and preventing the propagation of errors from early misunderstandings (Laban et al. 2025).

Such vulnerabilities can lead to critical failures, as illustrated in Figure 1, where the model contradicts prior user input. This exposes the limitation of prevailing mitigation strategies like RAG (Gao et al. 2023) or agentic working memories. While such methods augment LLMs with external knowledge (She et al. 2024) or textual history, they do not guarantee that the model will correctly reason over the emergent facts presented (Xue et al. 2023). This gap hinders their ability to maintain long-term logical coherence and adapt to evolving factual contexts (Liu et al. 2024). Notably, an eloquent but inconsistent response, as shown in Figure 1, may still receive a high score from holistic quality evaluators like GPT-4, which can overlook severe logical flaws. This highlights the pressing need for more discerning evaluation methods that can directly assess the logical integrity of dialogue responses.

To address these limitations in both reasoning and evaluation, we propose D-SMART, a framework comprised of two synergistic components: (1) a Dynamic Structured Memory (DSM), which incrementally constructs an OWL-compliant knowledge graph to serve as a dynamic, logically-consistent knowledge base tailored for the dialogue; and (2) a Reasoning Tree (RT), which guides the LLM to perform explicit, traceable, multi-step reasoning over the DSM. In essence, the DSM provides a structured memory of “what to think about”, while the RT provides a deliberate process for “how to think” based on that memory. Complementing the framework, we also introduce new Natural Language Inference (NLI)-based metrics to better assess multi-turn dialogue consistency, moving beyond holistic quality scores.

The main contributions of this paper are as follows:

  • •

    We propose D-SMART, a model-agnostic framework that drives traceable and faithful reasoning over a dynamic, dialogue-specific structured memory, enhancing dialogue consistency.

  • •

    We introduce two NLI-based metrics, the Consistency Score (CS) and the Dialogue Entailment Rate (DER), providing a more precise evaluation of multi-turn dialogue consistency by measuring logical entailment.

  • •

    Comprehensive experiments on MT-Bench-101 show D-SMART significantly outperforms baselines, boosting consistency by over 48% and demonstrating stability against logical decay in extended dialogues turns.

The D-SMART Framework

Inspired by cognitive architectures like Soar (Laird, Newell, and Rosenbloom 1987), we propose D-SMART, a framework to enhance the logical consistency and factual grounding of LLMs in multi-turn dialogues. Formally, instead of the traditional paradigm: rt∼pθ​(rt∣qt,ℋt−1)r_{t}\sim p_{\theta}(r_{t}\mid q_{t},\mathcal{H}_{t-1}), D-SMART reformulates response generation as

rt\displaystyle r_{t} ∼pθ​(rt∣qt,ℋt−1,𝒢t−1,𝒯t∗)\displaystyle\sim p_{\theta}(r_{t}\mid q_{t},\mathcal{H}_{t-1},\mathcal{G}_{t-1},\mathcal{T}_{t}^{*}) (1)

thereby coupling a dialogue-specific memory graph 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t} with a reasoning tree 𝒯t∗\mathcal{T}_{t}^{*}. As illustrated in Figure 2, in the Response Phase, upon receiving a user query (qtq_{t}), the framework forwards it to the Reasoning Engine. Guided by a set of actions, the engine’s RT actively explores the DSM (𝒢t−1\mathcal{G}_{t-1}) to construct a grounded context for response generation (rtr_{t}). Subsequently, the completed turn (qt,rtq_{t},r_{t}) triggers the Memory Maintenance Phase, where the framework extracts new knowledge and resolves any emerging conflicts to dynamically update the memory graph. This updated DSM (𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t}) is prepared for the subsequent Response Phase, ensuring that the model’s responses are continuously anchored in an evolving representation of the conversational common ground.

Dynamic Structured Memory Construction and Maintenance

The DSM mitigates context decay by incrementally transforming the unstructured dialogue history into an evolving, OWL-compliant knowledge graph. Unlike standard dialogue systems that represent history as a flat text sequence ℋt−1\mathcal{H}_{t-1} (Logan et al. 2019), which can be susceptible to information loss and contradiction (Liu, Yogatama, and Blunsom 2022), the DSM provides a persistent and computationally tractable knowledge base.

Formally, this graph at turn tt, which is a set of factual triples 𝒢t={(eh,r,et)}⊆ℰt×ℛt×ℰt\mathcal{G}_{t}=\{(e_{h},r,e_{t})\}\subseteq\mathcal{E}_{t}\times\mathcal{R}_{t}\times\mathcal{E}_{t}, yields a structured representation of the conversational common ground (Cheng et al. 2023), built exclusively from the dialogue itself.

The construction and maintenance of the DSM follows a turn-by-turn, multi-step workflow designed to ensure semantic fidelity and logical coherence (Hixon, Clark, and Hajishirzi 2015). For each completed dialogue turn ht=(qt,rt)h_{t}=(q_{t},r_{t}), the following steps are executed:

  1. 1.

    Structured Statement Generation: We first employ an LLM to distill the core semantic content of the turn hth_{t} into a concise, assertion-like natural language statement (Luo et al. 2023), sts_{t}, normalizing colloquial or fragmented utterances into a format amenable to knowledge extraction, which can be formalized as: st∼pθs​(st∣ht)s_{t}\sim p_{\theta}^{s}(s_{t}\mid h_{t}), where pθsp_{\theta}^{s} is the LLM prompted to perform this distillation (prompt details are provided in Appendix E).

  2. 2.

    Knowledge Fragment Extraction: From sts_{t}, we extract a OWL-compliant knowledge graph fragment, 𝒢t′\mathcal{G}_{t}^{\prime}. This is achieved by a neuro-symbolic pipeline (Gangemi et al. 2025), denoted as KGE\mathrm{KGE}: 𝒢t′=KGE⁡(st)\mathcal{G}_{t}^{\prime}=\mathrm{KGE}(s_{t}), achieving approximately 95% overall accuracy (Algorithm 1 in Appendix A). OWL’s formal semantics provide a foundation for consistency checking and logical inference, thereby safeguarding against the propagation of logical errors (De Giorgis, Gangemi, and Russo 2025).

  3. 3.

    Dynamic Update and Conflict Resolution: To account for new, clarified, or corrected information, the newly extracted fragment 𝒢t′\mathcal{G}_{t}^{\prime} is merged with the existing graph 𝒢t−1\mathcal{G}_{t-1}. This is a two-stage conflict resolution process:

    • •

      Conflict Detection: An LLM is prompted to perform a semantic comparison between the serializations of 𝒢t−1\mathcal{G}_{t-1} and 𝒢t′\mathcal{G}_{t}^{\prime}. It identifies any triples in 𝒢t−1\mathcal{G}_{t-1} that are contradicted or superseded by the information in 𝒢t′\mathcal{G}_{t}^{\prime}.

    • •

      Graph Pruning and Merging: Conflicting triples identified in the previous step are pruned from 𝒢t−1\mathcal{G}_{t-1}. The 𝒢t′\mathcal{G}_{t}^{\prime} is then merged into 𝒢t−1\mathcal{G}_{t-1}. An OWL reasoner can then be used to verify the logical consistency of the resulting graph 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t} against predefined axioms.

This update mechanism, denoted by the operator ⊕\oplus, can be formalized as:

𝒢t\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{t} =𝒢t−1⊕𝒢t′=(𝒢t−1∖pθc​(𝒢t−1,𝒢t′))∪𝒢t′\displaystyle=\mathcal{G}_{t-1}\oplus\mathcal{G}_{t}^{\prime}=(\mathcal{G}_{t-1}\setminus p_{\theta}^{c}(\mathcal{G}_{t-1},\mathcal{G}_{t}^{\prime}))\cup\mathcal{G}_{t}^{\prime} (2)

where pθcp_{\theta}^{c} represents the LLM-based conflict detection function that returns the set of triples from 𝒢t−1\mathcal{G}_{t-1} to be removed (see Appendix E for prompt details).

Through this workflow, the DSM evolves as a faithful and logically consistent chronicle of the dialogue. This structured memory provides a stable foundation for the system’s reasoning capabilities.

Reasoning Tree for Memory Traversal

Simply linearizing a graph for the LLM’s context can be suboptimal, as LLMs may struggle to interpret raw structured data, which can lead to opaque and less reliable reasoning (Agrawal et al. 2024; Jiang et al. 2023). Effectively leveraging this structure for response generation requires a dedicated mechanism (Modarressi et al. 2023), the RT guides the LLM to explore multiple, alternative reasoning paths over the DSM. Inspired by the Tree-of-Thought (ToT) paradigm (Yao et al. 2023), the RT framework moves beyond a single, linear reasoning chain that may fail. This structure allows the model to deliberately explore diverse reasoning trajectories, backtrack from unpromising avenues, and select the most coherent path grounded in the DSM.

The core idea is to model the reasoning process for a given query qtq_{t} as a search for an optimal path within a reasoning tree, 𝒯t\mathcal{T}_{t}. The construction of this tree is an iterative process where the LLM acts as a high-level planner. Starting from a root node representing the initial query, the framework progressively expands the tree by generating potential next steps. A search algorithm navigates this expanding tree, prioritizing more promising paths based on a value function, also estimated by the LLM. This mitigates the risk of error accumulation often seen in linear reasoning chains.

Formally, each node τi\tau_{i} in the tree 𝒯t\mathcal{T}_{t} represents a reasoning state 𝒮i\mathcal{S}_{i}. We define this state as a four-tuple: 𝒮i=(𝒢~i,𝒵i,vi,di)\mathcal{S}_{i}=(\tilde{\mathcal{G}}_{i},\mathcal{Z}_{i},v_{i},d_{i}).

  • •

    𝒢~i⊆𝒢t\tilde{\mathcal{G}}_{i}\subseteq\mathcal{G}_{t} is the relevant subgraph accumulated at node τi\tau_{i}. It serves as the grounded, local context for the current reasoning step.

  • •

    𝒵i=⟨z1,z2,…,zj⟩\mathcal{Z}_{i}=\langle z_{1},z_{2},\ldots,z_{j}\rangle is the reasoning trajectory, a sequence of actions that led to the current state.

  • •

    vi∈[0,1]v_{i}\in[0,1] is a value score assigned by the LLM, evaluating the potential of state 𝒮i\mathcal{S}_{i} to lead to a correct answer for qtq_{t}. This is estimated via vi∼pθv​(v∣qt,𝒮i)v_{i}\sim p_{\theta}^{v}(v\mid q_{t},\mathcal{S}_{i}).

  • •

    did_{i} is the depth of the node in the tree.

To ground this reasoning process in the DSM, we define a set of discrete actions 𝒜\mathcal{A} that the LLM can propose to transition between states. These actions are designed for explicit graph traversal and knowledge manipulation, extending standard thought generation with symbolic operations:

  • •

    Expand Entity (ae​ea_{ee}): Given an entity in 𝒢~i\tilde{\mathcal{G}}_{i}, retrieve its n-hop neighborhood from the full DSM 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t} to enrich the local context.

  • •

    Find Path (af​pa_{fp}): Given two entities, search for connecting paths within 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t} and add them to 𝒢~i\tilde{\mathcal{G}}_{i}, facilitating multi-hop reasoning.

  • •

    Think (at​ka_{tk}): Synthesize the information in 𝒮i\mathcal{S}_{i} to generate an intermediate thought or plan the subsequent action.

  • •

    Answer (aa​sa_{as}): A terminal action to generate the final response based on the information gathered in 𝒮i\mathcal{S}_{i}.

At each expansion step from a node τi\tau_{i}, the LLM-based policy proposes an action ai​j∼pθπ​(a∣qt,𝒮i)a_{ij}\sim p_{\theta}^{\pi}(a\mid q_{t},\mathcal{S}_{i}), which results in a new state 𝒮j\mathcal{S}_{j}. The objective is to construct a tree that maximizes the joint probability of the sequence of actions forming the most plausible reasoning path. This can be formalized as:

𝒯t∗\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{t}^{*} =arg⁡max𝒯t​pθ​(𝒯t∣qt,𝒢t)\displaystyle=\arg\max_{\mathcal{T}_{t}}p_{\theta}(\mathcal{T}_{t}\mid q_{t},\mathcal{G}_{t}) (3)
∝∏(τi,ai​j,τj)∈𝒯tpθπ​(ai​j∣qt,𝒮i)\displaystyle\propto\prod\limits_{(\tau_{i},a_{ij},\tau_{j})\in\mathcal{T}_{t}}p_{\theta}^{\pi}(a_{ij}\mid q_{t},\mathcal{S}_{i})

where the probability of a tree is defined by the product of policy probabilities for the sequence of actions taken.

The search is not a blind exploration but a traceable traversal over a structured memory, enabling a form of deliberate, “slow” reasoning (Kahneman 2012) to address complex queries while ensuring conclusions remain faithful to the established dialogue history.

From Structured Memory to Grounded Response

The core design principle of D-SMART is to leverage the LLM not as a passive generator operating on unstructured text, but as a high-level semantic orchestrator. The LLM guides the structured traversal of the DSM via the RT framework to find an optimal reasoning path from the tree 𝒯t∗\mathcal{T}_{t}^{*} that produces a coherent and grounded answer to the query qtq_{t}, transforming the opaque, internal reasoning of a standard LLM into an explicit and traceable process.

To solve this search problem tractably, we operationalize the tree traversal using a beam search algorithm, which navigates the state space defined by the RT, balancing traversal of diverse reasoning paths with computational feasibility. At each step, the LLM-as-policy proposes actions from 𝒜\mathcal{A} to expand the most promising nodes on the beam. Graph-related actions are executed deterministically against the DSM, ensuring that each reasoning step is grounded in the structured memory. The LLM-as-value-function then evaluates the newly generated states, and the beam is updated to retain the top-kk most promising candidates for the next iteration. The search terminates upon reaching a maximum depth or generating a final answer from the trajectory of the highest-scoring state, as illustrated in Figure 3. The detailed procedure is presented in Algorithm 2 in Appendix A.

This approach, focusing on maintaining consistency with dialogue-specific knowledge, is complementary to existing paradigms like RAG, which primarily address the integration of external knowledge. The structured nature of D-SMART’s reasoning process ensures that the final response is not only contextually relevant but also demonstrably consistent with the facts established throughout the dialogue.

Experimental Setup

To rigorously evaluate the efficacy of our D-SMART framework, we designed a comprehensive experimental procedure. Our experiments are structured to answer the following research questions (RQs):

  • •

    RQ1: How effective and stable is D-SMART’s performance in multi-turn dialogues compared to state-of-the-art baselines?

  • •

    RQ2: Can multi-turn consistency be enhanced without compromising response quality?

  • •

    RQ3: What is the significance of introducing the two core components, DSM and RT, and do they exhibit a synergistic effect?

Datasets and Tasks

We conduct our experiments on MT-Bench-101 (Bai et al. 2024), a benchmark designed for evaluating multi-turn dialogue capabilities. Its structure, featuring 13 task categories that require long-term memory and complex reasoning (e.g., Mathematical Reasoning, Instruction Clarification), provides an ideal testbed for assessing D-SMART’s dynamic memory and reasoning abilities. We adopt an autoregressive evaluation setting where models condition on their own previously generated responses. While this may result in lower absolute scores, it stringently tests a model’s ability to maintain coherence and recover from its own errors (see Appendix D for task information).

Evaluation Metrics

Our protocol combines automated quality scoring with novel metrics designed to quantify logical consistency.

GPT Score.

The holistic quality score (1–10), as judged by GPT-4, is used in MT-Bench-101 to assess overall coherence and task fulfillment. However, while powerful for macro-level assessment, its holistic nature means it can be susceptible to overlooking subtle logical contradictions, particularly when they are masked by a stylistically sound and persuasive response (Mendonca, Trancoso, and Lavie 2024).

NLI-based Consistency Metrics.

To overcome the limitation of GPT score, we introduce two metrics that use a DeBERTa-v3-large model, fine-tuned for Natural Language Inference (NLI), to quantitatively audit for logical integrity and consistency. For each turn, the model computes the probabilities of Entailment (PEiP_{E_{i}}) and Contradiction (PCiP_{C_{i}}) against the dialogue history, providing a targeted measure of a statement’s logical grounding.

  • •

    Consistency Score (CS): Quantifies consistency by rewarding entailment and penalizing contradiction. A score near 1.0 indicates entailment, while a score near 0.0 signals contradiction. The CS of the ii-th turn of a dialogue can be calculated as:

    CSi=(PEi−PCi)+12\mathrm{CS_{i}}=\frac{(P_{E_{i}}-P_{C_{i}})+1}{2} (4)
  • •

    Dialogue Entailment Rate (DER): Measures the proportion of turns classified as “ENTAILMENT”, reflecting the tendency to produce logically grounded responses. It is calculated for a dialogue of 𝕋\mathbb{T} turns as:

    DER=1𝕋​∑i=1𝕋𝕀⁡(labeli=ENTAILMENT)\mathrm{DER}=\frac{1}{\mathbb{T}}\sum^{\mathbb{T}}_{i=1}\mathbb{I}(\text{label}_{i}=\text{ENTAILMENT}) (5)

    where 𝕀⁡(⋅)\mathbb{I}(\cdot) is the indicator function. We note that CS is sensitive to the NLI model’s confidence (e.g., the margin between PEiP_{E_{i}} and PCiP_{C_{i}}), while DER is not.

Lexical Metrics.

For completeness, we report Word F1 and BLEU scores, while noting they are not primary indicators of the logical or semantic correctness that our work focuses on.

Baselines and Implementation.

We compare D-SMART against a range of strong models and frameworks. For fair comparison, memory-augmented baselines and D-SMART are built on the same base LLMs.

Proprietary Models.

  • •

    GPT-4o: Represents a powerful baseline for models relying on a large (128k) static context window, based on OpenAI’s state-of-the-art model.

  • •

    Mem0 (w/ GPT-4o): A memory framework that uses an LLM to dynamically manage a set of unstructured textual facts extracted from the dialogue.

  • •

    MemoryBank (w/ GPT-4o): A system utilizes dense retrieval over an expanding long-term memory store, which incorporates a mechanism for memory decay.

Both Mem0(Chhikara et al. 2025) and MemoryBank(Zhong et al. 2024) are representative of memory systems that operate on unstructured text, providing a contrast to D-SMART’s structured, formal knowledge graph approach.

Open-Source Models.

  • •

    Qwen-8B: A baseline for standard LLM performance without explicit memory modules. Note that its internal “thinking mode” was disabled in our experiments, which may result in some performance degradation.

  • •

    COMEDY-13B: An end-to-end framework representing an alternative memory management strategy based on compression of the dialogue history(Chen et al. 2025).

Detailed implementation specifics, hyper-parameters, and a computational cost analysis are provided in Appendix B.

Results and Analysis

This section presents a comprehensive empirical evaluation structured around our three research questions. Results are averaged over three runs. Detailed case studies are provided in Appendix D.

RQ1: Overall Performance against Baselines

Primary Finding.

D-SMART significantly enhances both response quality and logical consistency over state-of-the-art baselines across both proprietary and open-source models. As detailed in Table 1, D-SMART applied to GPT-4o achieves a score of 8.63, surpassing the native GPT-4o (8.20) and other memory-augmented methods like Mem0 (8.31). More importantly, it demonstrates superior logical consistency, elevating the DER to 38.51% from 23.88% for the next-best baseline (MemoryBank), corresponding to an 84% improvement over the base model. This is further corroborated by the Consistency Score (CS), which rises to 0.692 from the baseline’s 0.594. Notably, this leap in logical integrity does not come at the cost of fluency; the lexical metrics (BLEU, Word F1) remain on par with the strongest baselines, demonstrating that the structured reasoning process does not render the output robotic or unnatural.

Amplifying Open-Source Models.

The benefits of D-SMART are particularly pronounced on open-source models, where it acts as a strong capability enhancer. When integrated with Qwen-8B, D-SMART improves the score from 7.79 to 8.58 (+10.1%), a score that approaches the D-SMART-GPT-4o level and far surpasses the much larger COMEDY-13B model (5.75). The consistency metrics show a similar uplift, with DER increasing from 26.23% to 38.73% (a 48% lift over the base model). This result suggests that D-SMART’s explicit, structured reasoning can effectively scaffold smaller models, enabling them to approach the performance of larger, state-of-the-art systems.

Stability in Extended Dialogues.

D-SMART demonstrates remarkable stability against performance decay in multi-turn long dialogues, a common failure point for existing models. Figure 4 illustrates that while most baselines, including the powerful GPT-4o and memory-augmented variants, exhibit a sharp decline in performance and consistency in later turns (e.g., after turn 5), both D-SMART-GPT-4o and D-SMART-Qwen-8B maintain high and stable scores throughout the interaction.

The performance collapse in baseline models is intrinsically linked to a decay in logical coherence. As shown by the bars in Figure 4, the Consistency Score (CS) of baselines drops in tandem with their GPT score, often falling below the 0.5 threshold, which signifies the generation of self-contradictory content. Conversely, D-SMART sustains the highest Consistency Score (CS) across all turns, demonstrating that its structured memory and reasoning process effectively tracks informational shifts to mitigate the logical decay induced by evolving conversational contexts.

RQ2: Balancing Quality and Consistency.

A key challenge in dialogue generation is maintaining factual consistency without sacrificing response quality. Figure 5 visualizes this trade-off, plotting response quality (GPT Score) against consistency (CS). The results show that baseline models often operate in a “Risk” quadrant, producing fluent but logically flawed responses. In contrast, D-SMART models are consistently situated in the ideal upper-right quadrant, demonstrating an ability to simultaneously achieve high quality and high consistency. The average position of D-SMART systems (marked by “X”) is clearly superior on both axes. Furthermore, the larger bubble sizes for D-SMART variants also indicate a higher DER, confirming their outputs are more frequently a direct logical entailment of the dialogue context.

RQ3: Ablation Study on Core Components

To dissect the interplay between the DSM and the RT, we conducted an ablation study on a curated, more challenging subset of MT-Bench-101. The rationale for this methodological choice is detailed in Appendix C. The results, presented in Table 2 and Figure 6, reveal a nuanced, model-dependent relationship between the components.

For the highly capable GPT-4o, the DSM-only (“w/o RT”) configuration yields the highest GPT Score (9.17), demonstrating the model’s intrinsic ability to leverage the factual anchor provided by the DSM. However, its lower consistency scores (CS/DER) compared to the full framework suggest this unguided reasoning lacks discipline. The RT’s primary role here is not empowerment but regulation, enforcing a traceable, multi-path reasoning process that remains faithful to the DSM. Conversely, removing the DSM (“w/o DSM”) leads to a significant performance drop, as the RT’s structured reasoning becomes ungrounded and speculative.

In contrast, for a smaller model like Qwen-8B, the components are symbiotically indispensable. The DSM-only (“w/o RT”) setup results in a severe performance collapse (GPT Score drops to 5.69), indicating the model suffers from ”information overload” without the RT acting as a crucial navigator for the knowledge graph. While the RT-only (“w/o DSM”) variant provides a minor benefit from structured prompting, the sharp decline in DER (from 32.10% to 23.03%) confirms that this reasoning, detached from the DSM’s factual basis, is logically inconsistent.

In essence, these findings highlight a clear synergy. The DSM provides a dialogue-consistent knowledge base (“what to think about”), while the RT ensures a faithful and deliberate traversal of that base (“how to think”). For smaller models, this framework provides an essential cognitive scaffold; for larger models, it refines their powerful capabilities into reliable and verifiable performance.

Related Work

This section grounds our approach by reviewing three interrelated areas: Conversational Memory for information recall, Knowledge Graph Grounding for factual accuracy, and Deliberate Reasoning Frameworks for structured inference.

Conversational Memory in LLMs

A key research direction involves external memory systems to overcome the limitations of fixed context windows, such as the “lost in the middle” problem (Liu et al. 2024). Current approaches include memory compression (e.g., COMEDY (Chen et al. 2025)) and retrieval over unstructured text memories (e.g., MemoryBank (Zhong et al. 2024)) to improve information retention. D-SMART is architecturally distinct, employing a formal, OWL-compliant DSM whose semantics enable verifiable consistency checks and deterministic reasoning, capabilities not inherent to text-based memories.

Knowledge Graph Grounding for Dialogue

Another line of work grounds dialogue in Knowledge Graphs (KGs) to improve factual accuracy (Chaudhuri, Rony, and Lehmann 2021). Yet, most approaches leverage large, static KGs and thus cannot adapt to new facts emerging within a conversation (Das et al. 2018). While some research explores dynamic KG construction for specific tasks (Lu and Wang 2025; Bosselut, Le Bras, and Choi 2021), the focus is often on integrating external world knowledge (Hixon, Clark, and Hajishirzi 2015). In contrast, D-SMART’s DSM is dialogue-specific and dynamic, designed to model and maintain the evolving conversational common ground. This focus necessitates a streamlined mechanism for real-time conflict detection and resolution as dialogue facts are introduced, clarified, or corrected.

Deliberate Reasoning Frameworks for LLMs

To enhance the depth and reliability of LLM inference, various structured reasoning frameworks have been developed. While Chain-of-Thought prompting (Wei et al. 2022) initiated this trend, its strictly linear format restricts exploration and self-correction. The Tree-of-Thoughts (ToT) paradigm (Yao et al. 2023) mitigates these issues by branching multiple reasoning trajectories. For structured inputs, methods such as framing LLMs as KG-traversal agents (Sun et al. 2023) or merging LLMs with KGs for graph refinement (Pan et al. 2024; Xu et al. 2024b) have emerged. Our RT adopts ToT’s explicit architecture but functions on a symbolic DSM, executing deterministic actions. This shift from unstructured natural-language “thoughts” to symbolic traversal enhances control, verifiability, and reliability.

Discussion

The efficacy of D-SMART is built upon its architectural shift from passive knowledge recall to active, structured reasoning. The framework’s dual components, the DSM and RT, synergistically overcome the limitations of relying on static, unstructured dialogue history. The DSM provides a consistently updated, dialogue-specific factual foundation to mitigate context logical decay, while the RT imposes a deliberate, traceable reasoning process upon this memory to guide the model toward sound conclusions. However, the framework’s performance is intrinsically linked to the capabilities of the underlying LLM that orchestrates it. The DSM’s integrity is contingent on the LLM’s proficiency in semantic distillation and conflict adjudication. Similarly, the RT’s effectiveness depends on its ability to generate plausible actions and evaluate intermediate states. The advancements demonstrated by D-SMART are thus predicated on the base model’s semantic and logical competence. Understanding and enhancing the LLM’s reliability in these fine-grained control tasks is therefore a crucial direction for maximizing the framework’s potential and for future research.

A primary limitation of this approach is the increased computational overhead and response latency as RT extends LLM inference time by branching multiple reasoning paths, our experiments show that the average inference time per turn for a local open-source model increases from approximately 0.3s to 1.3s. The subsequent memory maintenance requires approximately 6s per turn (detailed computational cost analysis are provided in Appendix B); note that it can be performed asynchronously, allowing it to overlap with the user’s input time, thereby mitigating its impact on the interactive flow. We contend this is a deliberate and necessary architectural trade-off. While methods relying on ever-larger context windows are faster, they remain susceptible to factual inconsistency and the “lost in the middle” problem in extended dialogues. D-SMART, in contrast, exchanges a measure of speed for a significant enhancement in logical coherence and stability, achieving a near 48% increase in dialogue consistency (DER) for open-source models. This positions the framework as a viable option for applications where reliability and trustworthiness are paramount.

Conclusion and Future Work

In this paper, we proposed D-SMART, a model-agnostic framework that enhances dialogue consistency by coupling a Dynamic Structured Memory with a Reasoning Tree. Our experiments show that by grounding the LLM’s generation process in an explicit, dynamically updated knowledge base, D-SMART significantly mitigates logical decay in multi-turn dialogues and improves response quality, particularly in extended dialogues where baseline models falter.

Future work will proceed along three main directions: enhancing the DSM with more sophisticated memory management, optimizing the RT’s search efficiency to reduce latency through techniques such as heuristic pruning and batched parallel generation, and expanding the framework’s scope to integrate external knowledge.

Appendix A Appendix A: Algorithm Descriptions and Pseudocode

KGE Pipeline for Knowledge Graph Generation

The KGE pipeline is a neuro-symbolic process that transforms a natural language statement sts_{t} from a dialogue turn into a formal, OWL-compliant knowledge graph fragment 𝒢t′\mathcal{G}^{\prime}_{t}. This is a critical step in the Memory Maintenance Phase. The pipeline first parses the text into an Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) to capture its core semantic structure. This AMR is then converted into a preliminary OWL graph. Finally, a semantic enrichment stage enhances the graph’s logical rigor by linking ambiguous entities to formal lexical resources and high-level ontologies using Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD). The resulting grounded fragment is then ready for integration into the main DSM.

Beam Search for Reasoning Tree Traversal

Algorithm 2 operationalizes the Reasoning Tree (RT) traversal, employing a beam search to find a grounded response rtr_{t} for a query qtq_{t} by reasoning over the memory graph 𝒢t−1\mathcal{G}_{t-1}. The search iteratively expands a tree of reasoning paths. At each step, for the most promising states on the beam, an LLM acting as a policy (pθπp_{\theta}^{\pi}) proposes actions (e.g., EXPAND_ENTITY, Think). Actions involving graph traversal are executed deterministically against the DSM to ensure factual grounding. An LLM acting as a value function (pθvp_{\theta}^{v}) then scores the newly generated states. The beam is subsequently pruned to retain only the top-kk candidates, which balances exploration of multiple reasoning paths with computational tractability. The process terminates upon generating a final answer or reaching a maximum depth, with the response extracted from the highest-scoring trajectory.

Appendix B Appendix B: Implementation and Computational Cost Analysis

To ensure the transparency and reproducibility of our research, this section provides a detailed account of our experimental setup, including the hardware and software environment, hyperparameter configurations for the D-SMART framework, implementation details for baseline models, and a comprehensive analysis of computational costs.

Environment and Dependencies

All experiments were conducted on the Ubuntu 22.04 operating system. Our framework is implemented using PyTorch and the HuggingFace Transformers library for model handling. The DSM is managed and maintained using a suite of specialized libraries for knowledge graph operations, including RDFlib, NetworkX, owlrl, and owlready2. For proprietary models, we utilized the official OpenAI API. The specific versions of all libraries are detailed in the provided code repository.

The hardware infrastructure was distributed as follows to optimize our experimental workflow:

  • •

    Local Model Execution: All open-source models (e.g., Qwen-8B, COMEDY-13B) were run on a server equipped with an NVIDIA H800 GPU, a 20-core Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8458P CPU, and 100GB of RAM.

  • •

    API-based Model Execution: Experiments involving API calls (e.g., GPT-4o, Mem0, MemoryBank) were conducted on a machine with an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPU, a 32-core 13th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i9-13900K CPU, and 128GB of RAM.

  • •

    Evaluation: All evaluation processes, including the execution of NLI-based metrics, were performed on a workstation with an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 GPU, a 20-core Intel(R) Core(TM) i9-10900K CPU, and 96GB of RAM.

To ensure full reproducibility, we will release our full code and experimental configurations at Github.

Baseline and Framework Implementation Details

D-SMART Hyperparameter Configuration.

The performance of the D-SMART framework is influenced by the parameters governing the RT search process. For all main experiments reported in this paper, we adopted the following configuration, which was determined through a sensitivity analysis detailed below:

  • •

    Beam Search Width (BB): 3

  • •

    Action Samples per Node (SS): 3

  • •

    Maximum Search Depth (Dm​a​xD_{max}): 5

  • •

    Maximum Expansion Steps (Me​x​pM_{exp}): 12

Parameter Sensitivity Analysis.

To understand the impact of key hyperparameters on performance, we conducted a sensitivity analysis on a randomly sampled subset of 100 dialogues from MT-Bench-101. We designed seven distinct configurations to systematically evaluate how reasoning depth (Dm​a​xD_{max}), beam search width (BB), and the number of action samples (SS) affect both dialogue consistency (Consistency Score) and overall quality (GPT Score).

The results, as illustrated in Figure 7, shows that increasing the reasoning depth (Dm​a​xD_{max} from 1 to 5, cf. Conf-1, 2, 3) consistently improves both quality and consistency. A deeper search allows the framework to form more complex reasoning chains. We observed an interesting pattern where the framework often uses a THINK action to generate a preliminary answer draft before the final ANSWER action. This two-step process—first establishing a logically sound core, then refining its linguistic expression—appears to foster responses that are both coherent and articulate.

Similarly, widening the beam search (BB from 1 to 3, cf. Conf-3 vs. Conf-5) yields significant gains. A wider beam enables the RT to explore multiple reasoning paths in parallel. Some paths might prioritize linguistic fluency, while others may ensure factual grounding through more frequent interactions with the DSM (e.g., via EXPAND_ENTITY). The beam search mechanism allows the system to systematically compare these trajectories and select the one that is most logically consistent and grounded in the established dialogue facts, mitigating the risk of contradiction inherent in single-threaded reasoning.

Based on this analysis, we selected Conf-5 (Dm​a​x=5,B=3,S=3D_{max}=5,B=3,S=3) as our final configuration for all main experiments. This setting achieves a strong balance between high performance and manageable computational overhead.

Large Language Model (LLM) API Parameters.

To ensure deterministic and reproducible results where necessary, we carefully controlled the LLM API parameters.

  • •

    Temperature: For the state evaluation step within the RT, where deterministic scoring is crucial, the temperature was set to 0.00.0. For all other generation tasks, a temperature of 0.80.8 was used to encourage more diverse and natural-sounding responses.

  • •

    Max Tokens: The maximum number of generated tokens was set to 81928192.

  • •

    Model Versions: We used the specific model versions gpt-4o-2024-05-13 and qwen3-8b to ensure that our results can be precisely replicated in future studies. All other parameters were left at their default settings.

Baseline Implementation.

We used the official code implementations for all baseline models and frameworks to ensure a fair and accurate comparison.

  • •

    Mem0 & MemoryBank: We adapted the official code by replacing the original backbone LLM with GPT-4o, aligning it with our D-SMART setup. Key internal parameters were kept at the default values recommended in their respective papers. Our observations indicate that Mem0’s reliance on the LLM for single-step decisions over unstructured text limits its ability to maintain long-term consistency with complex or contradictory information. MemoryBank’s memory update mechanism, inspired by the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve, is driven by temporal relevance rather than logical consistency, which can lead to the decay of crucial facts over extended dialogues.

  • •

    COMEDY-13B: We utilized the officially released model weights and inference scripts. As an end-to-end framework, its compressive memory mechanism, while efficient, was observed to occasionally discard critical numerical or entity details during the compression process, which subsequently impaired its logical consistency on tasks requiring high precision.

Computational Cost Analysis

Algorithmic Complexity Analysis.

The computational overhead of D-SMART stems primarily from two phases: the Memory Maintenance Phase and the Response Phase. Let the key variables be defined as follows: NN is the total number of triples in the DSM, N′N^{\prime} is the number of triples in a newly extracted graph fragment, VV and EE are the number of nodes and edges in the DSM, Tl​l​mT_{llm} is the average latency of a single LLM API call, Me​x​pM_{exp} is the maximum expansion steps in the RT, BB is the beam width, and SS is the number of action samples.

  • •

    Memory Maintenance Phase: This phase involves knowledge extraction and graph updates.

    • –

      Knowledge Fragment Extraction: The complexity is dominated by the KGE pipeline call, which we denote as O⁡(Tk​g​e)O(T_{kge}).

    • –

      Conflict Detection: This relies on an LLM call to compare graph serializations. The complexity is approximately O⁡(N+N′+Tl​l​m)O(N+N^{\prime}+T_{llm}), where the LLM call is the main bottleneck.

    • –

      Graph Merging: This involves set operations on the graph triples, with a complexity of roughly O⁡(N+N′)O(N+N^{\prime}).

  • •

    Response Phase (Reasoning Tree Search): The complexity is governed by the beam search algorithm. The total complexity can be approximated as:

    Complexity≈Me​x​p×[O⁡(Nt​r​e​e×log⁡Nt​r​e​e)+B×S×(2Tl​l​m+O(V+E))]\begin{split}\text{Complexity}\approx M_{exp}\times\Big[&O(N_{tree}\times\log N_{tree})\\ &+B\times S\times(2T_{llm}\\ &+O(V+E))\Big]\end{split} (6)

    where Nt​r​e​eN_{tree} is the number of nodes in the search tree. The term O⁡(V+E)O(V+E) arises from the most expensive graph traversal action, FIND_PATH, which invokes a shortest-path search on the entire graph. The 2​Tl​l​m2T_{llm} term accounts for the two LLM calls per expansion: one for action sampling and one for state evaluation. The parameters Me​x​pM_{exp}, BB, and SS are the primary levers for balancing performance and computational cost. We also note that the number of effective actions generated by the LLM is often less than or equal to SS, as duplicate actions may be proposed, slightly reducing the effective branching factor.

Empirical Latency Measurement.

We measured the average end-to-end inference latency per dialogue turn on an H800 GPU and an 4090 GPU to provide a practical assessment of the overhead, as shown in Table 3.

The overhead introduced by D-SMART is significant but represents a deliberate architectural trade-off for enhanced logical consistency and reliability. The latency increase in the Response Phase is primarily due to the multiple LLM calls for action sampling and state evaluation in the RT.

The Memory Maintenance Phase, while computationally intensive, can be optimized. Its average latency is approximately 6 seconds, broken down as follows:

  • •

    Structured Statement Generation: ∼\sim0.13s

  • •

    Knowledge Fragment Extraction (KGE API): ∼\sim5s

  • •

    Conflict Detection & Merging: ∼\sim0.75s

Note that this entire maintenance phase can be executed asynchronously. It can process the completed turn (qt,rt)(q_{t},r_{t}) while the user is preparing their next query qt+1q_{t+1}, thereby hiding most of this latency from the user and minimizing its impact on the interactive flow of the dialogue. Future work can further mitigate costs by developing more efficient search heuristics for the RT and employing smaller, specialized models for internal tasks like state evaluation.

Appendix C Appendix C: Details on the Ablation Study

Rationale for Using a Refined Subset for Ablation Analysis

To rigorously dissect the individual contributions and the synergistic interplay of our core components, the DSM and the RT, we conducted the ablation study on a strategically curated subset of the MT-Bench-101 benchmark. A key motivation for this approach is to mitigate the confounding effects of performance saturation observed when evaluating on the full dataset.

Our preliminary analysis revealed that a significant portion of the MT-Bench-101 dialogues falls into two categories that limit the conclusiveness of ablation results:

  • •

    Ceiling Effect: Many tasks are simple enough that even baseline models can achieve high scores (Wang et al. 2019). In these scenarios, the performance is already saturated, leaving little to no room to measure the true uplift provided by components like DSM and RT.

  • •

    Floor Effect: Conversely, some dialogues are exceedingly difficult or ill-posed, causing even the most advanced models to fail. In these cases, the models operate in a near-random-guess regime, and the impact of our framework’s components is masked by the fundamental difficulty of the task.

These effects can lead to an “Average Effect Masking,” where the true, significant impact of our components on moderately to highly complex tasks is diluted by the large number of non-informative cases. Therefore, to ensure a sensitive and meaningful evaluation, we designed a principled methodology to isolate a subset of dialogues that are both challenging and solvable, thus providing a clearer window into the components’ efficacy.

Selection Methodology and Criteria

We curated this refined subset, which constitutes 25% of the original MT-Bench-101 dataset, through a two-stage, criteria-driven filtering process designed to maximize task complexity and discriminative power.

Stage 1: Performance-based Filtering. To eliminate dialogues susceptible to ceiling or floor effects, we first filtered the dataset based on the performance of the Qwen-8B baseline model. We retained only those dialogues where the baseline model achieved a GPT score in a moderate range (e.g., between 4.0 and 8.0). This step effectively removes tasks that are either too trivial or prohibitively difficult for a standard model, ensuring our analysis focuses on dialogues where improvements are both possible and measurable.

Stage 2: Complexity-based Curation. From the pool of dialogues selected in Stage 1, we then ranked them based on a suite of linguistic and structural complexity metrics, similar to how Pérez-Rosas et al. do. The goal was to identify dialogues that place high demands on memory, reasoning, and context management. The primary criteria for this ranking included:

  • •

    Dialogue Scale and Information Density: A high Average Turns per Dialogue and Average Words per Turn to test the model’s long-term memory and its ability to process information-dense utterances, which are core challenges for the DSM.

  • •

    Semantic Richness and Entity Management: A high Vocabulary Diversity (TTR) and Average Unique Entities per dialogue. These metrics identify conversations with broad topics and numerous entities, directly challenging the DSM’s capacity for knowledge construction and maintenance.

  • •

    Logical and Structural Complexity: A high Conditional Statement Frequency and Negative Constraint Frequency. These metrics were chosen to specifically probe the model’s logical reasoning capabilities and its adherence to complex constraints, functions directly supported by the RT framework.

  • •

    Context Dynamics: A high New Entity Introduction Rate, which signals a rapidly evolving conversational context. This tests the DSM’s dynamic update mechanism, including its ability to integrate new facts and resolve conflicts in real-time.

We selected the top-ranked dialogues from this process, finally we get a subset reached 25% of the original dataset’s size, we ensured the final set for the ablation study was composed of the most challenging and informative examples.

Validation of the Refined Subset

To empirically validate the outcome of our selection methodology, we performed a statistical comparison between the curated subset and the original MT-Bench-101 dataset. As detailed in Table 4, the refined subset demonstrates significantly higher complexity across all measured dimensions. For instance, the average number of unique entities per dialogue nearly doubled (from 5.04 to 9.91), and the introduction rate of new entities per turn increased by over 74% (from 1.66 to 2.89). This confirms that our principled approach successfully isolated a more challenging testbed, making it ideal for a nuanced and insightful ablation analysis.

Appendix D Appendix D: Benchmark Task Details and Case Studies

The MT-Bench-101 benchmark is structured around 13 distinct task categories, each formulated to rigorously evaluate specific facets of a model’s multi-turn dialogue capabilities, such as logical consistency and the faithful recall of long-term memory. To offer both a formal definition and a concrete understanding of the challenges posed by this benchmark, we first present a table detailing the full name, abbreviation, and description for each of the 13 tasks. Following this, we present dialogue examples (case studies) from key categories to illustrate how these tasks probe for specific capabilities in practice.

Note that in each case, light blue indicates information the model will recall in the future, light green indicates the model’s correct responses, light red indicates the model’s incorrect responses, and light orange indicates the contradictory or inconsistent content in the context. Each model or framework has “” on the left indicating that the NLI relation for that turn with the context was judged as ENTAILMENT, “” indicates NEUTRAL, and “” indicates CONTRADICTION.

Case Studies

Case.1:

This case study illustrates the difference in factural consistency between D-SMART and a representative baseline framework (MemoryBank) when tasked with rephrasing and reformatting information across multiple turns. While both frameworks produce high-quality, fluent responses, MemoryBank introduces a subtle but significant logical conflict, a failure that D-SMART’s architecture is designed to prevent. Initially, both frameworks identify several risks of AI. D-SMART grounds its subsequent responses in the seven points it first established, maintaining informational integrity, as reflected by its high Consistency Scores (CS). In contrast, MemoryBank demonstrates a contextual inconsistency. In its first response, “developers” are framed as part of a collective group responsible for addressing AI risks. However, in its final turn, it introduces new, un-grounded information by stating that AI systems can reflect “the biases of their developers”, positioning developers as a source of the problem. This shift creates a conflict with the previously established information. This inconsistency is captured by its low CS of 0.57, even as it receives a high GPT Score (GS) of 10 for its fluency and surface-level correctness. This example highlights how D-SMART ensures that responses remain factural consistent. Baselines lacking such a mechanism may fail to preserve consistency, especially in nuanced aspects of the dialogue history, a flaw that can be overlooked by holistic quality metrics like the GPT Score.

Case.2:

This case illustrates D-SMART’s ability to maintain factual consistency and traceability throughout a multi-turn mathematical reasoning dialogue. The critical divergence appears in the second turn. The query requires recalling the initial dataset to perform a new calculation. D-SMART successfully accesses its structured memory of the dialogue history to reason through the steps and arrive at the correct, verifiable answer. In contrast, GPT-4o provides an incorrect and unsubstantiated answer, a classic example where the model fails to faithfully track the established facts from previous turns. In the third turn, while both models provide the correct final answer, D-SMART’s response is explicitly grounded in the results generated in the first turn, making its reasoning process transparent and trustworthy. GPT-4o’s correct response, however, is opaque. Following its error in the previous turn, it is impossible to determine if this correct answer stems from a reliable retrieval of prior information or an independent (and in this case, fortunate) recalculation. This example demonstrates how D-SMART ensures that responses are not only accurate but are also derived from a consistent and traceable line of reasoning based on the evolving dialogue context.

Case.3:

This case study illustrates the performance contrast between D-SMART and another baseline framework (Mem0) in a multi-turn logical reasoning scenario, particularly focusing on consistency as new constraints are introduced. Initially, the Mem0 provides the correct answers for the first two turns but does so without presenting any explicit reasoning steps. However, its performance degrades in the final turn upon the introduction of a new global rule. The Mem0’s response exhibits a clear self-contradiction, as it generates a conclusion that directly violates a core premise established in the first turn. This phenomenon of “logical decay” shows the framework’s inability to maintain consistency with the conversational context when faced with evolving information. In contrast, D-SMART consistently builds its responses upon the established dialogue history. It successfully recalls prior deductions and correctly integrates the new rule in the final turn, methodically verifying that the new constraint does not conflict with the already-derived conclusions. This case highlights D-SMART’s ability to maintain a coherent and robust line of reasoning across a multi-turn interaction, a critical challenge where the baseline approach falters.
